title: Judges 7:9–15
context: Judges 7:9–15 is the night before the battle. The LORD repeats his promise to Gideon and, knowing his fear, offers him a sign: if he is afraid, he may go down with his servant Purah to the Midianite camp and listen. There Gideon overhears a soldier telling a dream of a barley loaf that flattens a tent, and his companion interpreting it as the sword of Gideon. Gideon worships and returns to rally the three hundred. The scene shows God’s patience with a fearful servant and his control even over the thoughts of Israel’s enemies.

verses.text: That same night, the LORD said to him, “Arise, go down into the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Gideon, “Arise, go down into the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand.” Arminian readers note that God’s word comes first and calls for a response. The past tense frames the victory as certain from God’s side, while Gideon still has to step out in trust and act on what he has been told.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God speaks of the victory as already accomplished: “I have delivered it into your hand.” His purpose is settled before the battle begins. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an expression of God’s faithful promise, which grounds Gideon’s action and gives him every reason for confidence.

verses.text: But if you are afraid to go down, go with Purah your servant down to the camp.
verses.arminianNotes: “But if you are afraid to go down, go with Purah your servant.” Arminian readers note God’s tender realism. He knows Gideon’s fear and meets it with an offer of reassurance, rather than rebuke, inviting a fearful servant to take the next step with help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s gracious accommodation to his servant’s weakness, as with the fleece in 6:36–40. God not only commands but also supplies what is needed to obey. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing God’s patience with fearful faith, and both find comfort here for believers whose trust is real but fragile.

verses.text: You will hear what they say; and afterward your hands will be strengthened to go down into the camp.” Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outermost part of the armed men who were in the camp.
verses.arminianNotes: God promises, “afterward your hands will be strengthened,” and Gideon goes down with Purah. Arminian readers note that Gideon accepts the offer, admitting his fear by his action. God’s encouragement does not override Gideon’s will but works through his willingness to go and listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the strengthening comes from God, who has arranged what Gideon will hear. The courage Gideon needs is a gift. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God strengthening a weak servant through means, and both see Gideon’s going down, in spite of fear, as a real act of faith.

verses.text: The Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like locusts for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand which is on the seashore for multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy lies in the valley “like locusts for multitude,” with camels “as the sand which is on the seashore for multitude.” Arminian readers note that the description underlines the scale of the challenge facing three hundred men. The more overwhelming the enemy appears, the clearer it becomes that only God can give the victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the hyperbolic language of locusts and sand sharpens the contrast with Gideon’s tiny force. The narrative is building toward a victory that can only be ascribed to God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stressing the impossibility of the task in human terms and so magnifying the LORD’s deliverance.

verses.text: When Gideon had come, behold, there was a man telling a dream to his fellow. He said, “Behold, I dreamed a dream; and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian, came to the tent, and struck it so that it fell, and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon arrives just as a soldier tells a dream of “a cake of barley bread” that tumbles into the camp and flattens a tent. Arminian readers often note that barley bread, humble food, may suggest Israel’s lowly position against the tent-dwelling Midianites, though the text does not explain the image. The timing of Gideon’s arrival is part of God’s encouragement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence in the precise timing: Gideon arrives at the very moment the dream is told. God governs even the dreams and conversations of Israel’s enemies. Shared ground: both traditions read the dream as a sign from God given for Gideon’s sake, and both caution against pressing the symbolism beyond the interpretation the text itself provides in 7:14.

verses.text: His fellow answered, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel. God has delivered Midian into his hand, with all the army.”
verses.arminianNotes: The companion interprets the dream: “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon … God has delivered Midian into his hand.” Arminian readers note that the enemy already fears Gideon. The rumor of God’s work has spread, showing how God’s earlier acts have prepared the way for this battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the very words God spoke to Gideon in 7:9 now come from the mouth of an enemy soldier. God confirms his promise through an unlikely witness. Shared ground: both traditions read the interpretation as God’s gracious confirmation, and both note that the Midianites themselves attribute the coming defeat to God.

verses.text: It was so, when Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, that he worshiped. Then he returned into the camp of Israel and said, “Arise, for the LORD has delivered the army of Midian into your hand!”
verses.arminianNotes: When Gideon hears the dream and its interpretation, “he worshiped.” Arminian readers note that Gideon’s first response is worship, not strategy. His fear gives way to trust, and he returns to the camp with renewed confidence, calling the people to rise because “the LORD has delivered the army of Midian into your hand!”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gideon’s worship acknowledges that the victory is God’s before any battle is fought. His announcement repeats God’s own words from 7:9. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of faith strengthened by God’s word and sign, and both see worship as the fitting response to God’s promise.
